Q115843612.summary: Within an arched frame Christ sits frontally on a jewelled, lattice-backed throne, raising his right hand in blessing and holding a closed Gospel book, his name abbreviated IC XC on either side of his cross-nimbed head. Carved in Constantinople as the centre of a Byzantine triptych, the panel was later reused in a Mosan book binding, whose walrus-ivory strips with the evangelists' symbols appear above and below it in this photograph. It embodies the calm majesty of Christ as ruler and teacher.
facts: The Louvre explains that the plaque was originally the central element of a late-10th-century Byzantine triptych whose wings are lost; the gilded architectural frame and old marks attest to this.
It was reused as the centre of a Mosan binding with two walrus-ivory complements (Louvre OA 2591 and OA 2592).
Before entering the Louvre in 1882 it belonged to the collections of Charles Stein and Louis-Charles Timbal.
Q115843612.notes: Inv. OA 2590. The photograph shows the Byzantine panel together with the separate Mosan walrus-ivory strips above and below.

cur:monumental-aquileia-good-shepherd.summary: Within an octagonal frame in the great floor mosaic, a young shepherd in a short tunic carries a lamb across his shoulders and holds a panpipe (syrinx), while a goat or deer stands at his side. Set among panels of animals and birds, the figure presents Christ in the familiar pastoral image of the Good Shepherd, at a time when Christian art was still borrowing freely from Roman decorative imagery.
facts: The pavement belongs to the twin halls built by Bishop Theodore from 313 or a few years later; covering more than 760 square metres, it is described as the oldest and largest Christian mosaic in the West.
The basilica of Aquileia is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

cur:objects-darmstadt-koimesis-ivory.summary: The Virgin lies on her bier surrounded by the grieving apostles, Peter at her head and Paul bowing at her feet. Behind the bier Christ stands in a mandorla-like space, holding in his arms his Mother's soul in the form of a small swaddled child, while angels descend from above to carry it to heaven. The scene beautifully reverses the Nativity: the Son now cradles his Mother as she once cradled him.
facts: The Dormition (Koimesis) is not narrated in the New Testament but in later apocryphal accounts; it became one of the Twelve Great Feasts of the Byzantine Church, celebrated on 15 August (tradition).
Ivory plaques of the Koimesis were especially numerous in 10th-century Constantinople, and several were later set into Western book covers (type).

Q116274109.summary: Carved in deep relief on a curved section of elephant tusk, Christ sits enthroned within an oval mandorla dotted with circles, blessing with his right hand and holding a book, while angels on either side bear the mandorla upward. Below, the Virgin stands in the centre with her hands raised in prayer, flanked by the apostles, several holding books. The bold, stylised carving shows how the Ascension was pictured by Christian craftsmen in Egypt or Palestine in the early Islamic period.
facts: Radiocarbon analysis gives the ivory a date of 720–970 (95% probability), according to The Met.
It is kept in The Met's Department of Islamic Art, reflecting its origin in Egypt or Palestine under Islamic rule (accession 17.190.46, gift of J. Pierpont Morgan, 1917).
